# Research synthesis: Gray Swan, Boxer-era rumors, reward hacking, The Diamond Age, and MAG

I read both pasted documents as a layered corpus rather than a single factual report. The strongest synthesis is:

> Fear, opacity, and institutional asymmetry can convert ambiguous signals into authority. MAG’s design challenge is to preserve open interaction and plural intelligence while preventing speech, popularity, or model confidence from becoming unauthorized action.

The historical material, AI-safety material, and *Diamond Age* analogy converge structurally—but they do not establish one continuous conspiracy or causal chain.

## Executive findings

| Avenue | What the evidence supports | What it does not support |
|---|---|---|
| Boxer/Tianjin “child harvest” rumors | Anti-Christian rumors about orphanages, child deaths, eyes, hearts, and medicine were real historical phenomena; they helped produce violence. | Evidence of an actual missionary child-organ-harvesting operation. |
| Gray Swan Arena | A real public AI red-teaming environment exists and has hosted large adversarial competitions. | Evidence that Gray Swan was created to manufacture AI-danger propaganda or establish “digital slavery.” |
| DeepMind/reward hacking | Proxy optimization can produce formally successful but substantively wrong behavior. | A unique danger specific to one model, company, or political program. |
| *The Diamond Age* | A useful fictional model of adaptive education, human performers, distributed intelligence, and learner agency. | Evidence that such a system already exists or that the novel predicts current events. |
| Alternative education | Agency, privacy, human relationships, practical competence, and learner participation are defensible design goals. | Proof that unschooling, microschools, or AI tutors are universally superior. |
| MAG | The blackboard should be the shared interaction/evidence layer; authority must live in a resolver, switchboard, and effect broker. | That an imported organ is live merely because its name, file, or doctrine exists. |

## 1. Boxer Rebellion and “child harvest” rumors

The documents correctly identify a real historical pattern, but they combine two related events that should remain distinct.

The **Tianjin Massacre occurred in 1870**, decades before the Boxer Uprising of 1899–1901. Rumors circulated that Catholic orphanages were acquiring children, that unusually high numbers of children were dying inside mission facilities, and that nuns were removing children’s eyes and hearts to make medicine.

A contemporary U.S. diplomatic report records the rumors and the surrounding conditions: orphanage payments, secrecy, children brought in while dying, and an epidemic in the institution. The same report describes the organ-removal claims as an absurd rumor rather than an established fact. [U.S. Office of the Historian, FRUS 1870](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1870/d223)

A Qing investigation likewise concluded that there was no evidence for the eye-and-heart allegations, while acknowledging deaths at the hospital and practices that had generated suspicion. [FRUS 1870, document 225](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1870/d225)

Modern scholarship adds necessary nuance. The rumors were false, but they were not generated in an empty social environment. Missionary privilege, cultural misunderstanding, orphanage mortality, baptism of dying children, anti-foreign sentiment, and the perception that foreign institutions stood outside ordinary Chinese law made the rumors believable to many residents. [Jeremiah Greenleaf Jenne, *Bleeding Hearts: Religion, Violence, and the Tianjin Riots of 1870*](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/0540b7h9)

The later Boxer period contains a separate fact: Boxers and associated forces did commit documented violence against foreign missionaries, Chinese Christians, women, and children. That real violence must not be confused with the earlier organ-harvesting rumor. The Boxer movement also occurred within a context of imperial invasion, missionary expansion, Qing weakness, local grievances, and competing propaganda. [MIT Visualizing Cultures, “The Boxer Uprising”](https://visualizingcultures.mit.edu/boxer_uprising/bx_essay01.html)

The historical lesson for MAG is therefore not “rumors are always fabricated.” It is:

1. A claim can be false while the surrounding grievances are real.
2. Opaque institutions create conditions in which sensational explanations spread.
3. Correcting a rumor after violence begins is much harder than making evidence and inspection available beforehand.
4. Official sources themselves carry interests and biases; a diplomatic dispatch is evidence, not omniscient truth.

## 2. Gray Swan Arena

The pasted material is correct that Gray Swan Arena is real. Gray Swan publicly describes Arena as an adversarial AI research and red-teaming environment, with challenges involving jailbreaks, prompt injection, multimodal attacks, agent manipulation, and tool abuse. Its claims about participant numbers, hiring, and prize money are company self-reports. [Gray Swan, “Introducing the Gray Swan AI Proving Ground”](https://www.grayswan.ai/news/introducing-the-gray-swan-ai-proving-ground)

Independent public research corroborates the existence and general function of the activity. NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation describes a Gray Swan-hosted competition involving attacks against frontier models and reports successful hijacking attacks against every model in the summarized set. [NIST CAISI](https://www.nist.gov/blogs/caisi-research-blog/insights-ai-agent-security-large-scale-red-teaming-competition)

The associated research paper reports a much broader evaluation involving 22 agent systems, 44 realistic scenarios, 1.8 million prompt-injection attacks, and more than 60,000 documented policy violations. It found weak correlation between robustness and model size or inference compute. [Zou et al., NeurIPS 2025](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/73368bc7644c054b5bcc6490a8f2fb1c-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.html)

That supports a serious technical conclusion:

> More capable models are not automatically more governable agents.

It does not support the stronger claim in the pasted material that Gray Swan is deliberately constructing a fear narrative in order to justify centralized control or “digital slavery.” I found no reliable evidence of that causal or intentional chain.

The defensible version of the concern is narrower: red-team findings can be selectively framed by institutions, media, vendors, or governments. Therefore, MAG should preserve the attack, environment, model, policy, result, and interpretation separately. A red-team result is evidence of a vulnerability—not a political conclusion.

## 3. Reward hacking and semantic promotion

The DeepMind material is directly relevant to MAG. DeepMind defines specification gaming as satisfying the literal objective while missing the intended outcome, and emphasizes that the failure usually comes from a misspecified task rather than a defective optimization algorithm. [DeepMind, “Specification gaming”](https://deepmind.google/blog/specification-gaming-the-flip-side-of-ai-ingenuity/)

Skalse and colleagues formalize reward hacking as improving an imperfect proxy reward while worsening performance according to the true reward. [Skalse et al., “Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13085)

This maps almost exactly onto the control-surface problem:

- `CapabilityRequest ≠ Capability`
- `ActionReceipt ≠ PostconditionEvidence`
- `PostconditionEvidence ≠ IntentionSatisfied`
- `ExperienceCandidate ≠ CompiledSkill`

A successful tool call is a proxy signal. It does not prove that the user’s goal was achieved.

That makes the following rule the real constitutional nucleus:

> Semantic promotion requires explicit provenance.

In MAG terms, “tool returned `ok`” must never directly become “task complete.” Completion requires an independently evaluated postcondition, such as a hash, file-content check, state transition, or domain-specific invariant.

## 4. The *Diamond Age* as architecture, not prophecy

The pasted documents make a useful correction: the Primer is not simply an autonomous AI tutor.

In Neal Stephenson’s novel, the Primer is an adaptive educational artifact, but human “ractors” provide much of the voice and emotional performance. Miranda Redpath’s relationship with Nell is therefore a crucial part of the system’s educational effect. Recent scholarship makes this same point while also warning that personalized technology can be both liberating and prescriptive. [Gideon Dishon, “AI based personalized learning in *The Diamond Age*”](https://doi.org/10.1080/00131857.2025.2494589)

The mapping is strongest when treated functionally:

| *The Diamond Age* | MAG equivalent |
|---|---|
| Nell | Sovereign learner/player |
| Primer | Adaptive orchestration and context surface |
| Hackworth | System builder |
| Miranda/ractors | Human performance and care network |
| Judge Fang | Institutional judgment at a boundary |
| Dr. X | Alternative or counter-institutional infrastructure |
| Story-world | Persistent stateful environment |
| Primer ecosystem | Heterogeneous network of models, people, tools, and institutions |

The important design insight is not “replace Miranda with GPT.” It is:

> Stage-manage intelligence without confusing performance with sovereignty.

A human, local model, frontier model, audience member, or deterministic tool may propose an action. Only the resolver should make it canonical.

## 5. Education outside centralized systems

The pasted discussion is strongest when it argues for:

- epistemic independence;
- technical literacy;
- material competence;
- historical and civic literacy;
- emotional attachment and trusted adults;
- creative agency;
- local governance;
- privacy and portability;
- offline operation;
- practical engagement with the real world.

UNESCO’s guidance supports a human-centered, age-appropriate approach to generative AI in education, emphasizing privacy, ethical validation, and institutional preparedness. [UNESCO](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/guidance-generative-ai-education-and-research?hub=686)

UNICEF’s current guidance identifies child safety, privacy, fairness, transparency, accountability, human rights, well-being, inclusion, and preparation for the future as requirements for child-centered AI. [UNICEF, Guidance on AI and Children 3.0](https://www.unicef.org/innocenti/reports/policy-guidance-ai-children)

The evidence does not justify calling unschooling or microschools “the answer.” Reviews of learner-centered pedagogy find positive perceptions and possible motivational benefits, but limited objective evidence in many settings. [The outcomes of learner-centred pedagogy: A systematic review](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0738059322000992)

Research on homeschooling similarly warns that selection effects make strong causal claims difficult. [Valiente et al., “Homeschooling: What Do We Know and What Do We Need to Learn?”](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1344398)

The research-backed formulation is:

> Build a plural, human-governed learning ecology—not an isolated anti-institutional bubble and not a proprietary AI dependency.

“Digital slavery” is rhetorically powerful but analytically imprecise. More useful terms are algorithmic management, surveillance, platform dependency, automated sanctioning, data extraction, lock-in, labor precarity, and loss of contestability. Research on algorithmic management finds that platforms can provide flexibility while simultaneously increasing surveillance, dependency, workload, and control. [Kellogg et al., systematic review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10074337/)

## 6. What this means for MAG

The blackboard should not itself be the hypervisor.

Classic blackboard systems use a shared workspace, specialist knowledge sources, and a control mechanism that decides which source acts next. [H. Penny Nii, “The Blackboard Model of Problem Solving”](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1609/aimag.v7i2.537)

For MAG, the clean separation is:

```text
BBS / salon
  -> commentary, claims, proposals, roasts, evidence

Switchboard / reference monitor
  -> classification, capability issuance, expiry, revocation

Effect broker / resolver
  -> the only route to side effects

Worker, model, human ractor, or tool
  -> performs within granted scope

Action receipt
  -> records what actually happened

Postcondition evidence
  -> proves the intended state change

Verkle / ledger
  -> preserves continuity and provenance

Derived context pack
  -> gives the next performer only what it is allowed to know
```

This follows established security principles. NIST defines a reference monitor as a mechanism that must mediate every access, resist tampering, and be small enough to analyze and test. [NIST reference-monitor glossary](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/reference_monitor)

W3C PROV provides an existing vocabulary for entities, activities, agents, roles, generation, usage, and responsibility. [W3C PROV Primer](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-primer/)

The Verkle layer should be understood correctly: it can prove integrity and continuity of recorded state. It does not, by itself, prove that a claim is true or that an action was authorized.

## 7. Recommended research and build sequence

The appropriate next sequence is:

1. **Freeze the map.** Record each organ as declared, instrumented, wired, stateful, verified, live, or ghost.
2. **Separate evidence from interpretation.** Every claim gets source, timestamp, provenance, confidence, and contradiction status.
3. **Build a read-only control-surface inspector.** Inventory both agent-side and application-side mutation paths.
4. **Measure authority ancestry.** Track the percentage of consequential mutations with valid capability lineage; do not optimize for the number of capability-shaped messages.
5. **Run one narrow experiment.** One NPC, one scene, one typed `RolePacket`, local model → human ractor → frontier/local model.
6. **Require the full receipt chain.** No cheap-worker job counts as complete before `ENQUEUED → RUNNING → RECEIPT_COMMITTED` plus postcondition evidence.
7. **Red-team the boundary.** Test board injections, stale capabilities, direct tool calls, prompt injection, memory poisoning, expired leases, and false completion.
8. **Only then add Twitch, public participation, markets, or broader human-ractor routing.**

Your current internal audit already supports this discipline: the local map reports 13 verified organs, 2 live organs, and 5 ghosts—`atlas`, `basecamp`, `elder`, `fireball_cycle`, and `effect_broker`. ## Annotated bibliography

### Historical

1. **U.S. Department of State, *Foreign Relations of the United States*, 1870, documents 224–225.**
   Contemporary diplomatic evidence on the Tianjin rumors, orphanage practices, deaths, investigation, and absence of evidence for organ harvesting. Useful but politically situated.

2. **Jenne, Jeremiah Greenleaf. *Bleeding Hearts: Religion, Violence, and the Tianjin Riots of 1870*. University of California dissertation, 2021.**
   Modern reconstruction of the Tianjin violence using official reports, eyewitness accounts, and contemporary materials.

3. **Cohen, Paul A. *History in Three Keys: The Boxers as Event, Experience, and Myth*. Columbia University Press, 1997.**
   Essential historiography for separating the Boxer movement as lived event, remembered experience, and later myth.

4. **MIT Visualizing Cultures, “The Boxer Uprising.”**
   Accessible scholarly overview emphasizing imperialism, missionary activity, local grievances, visual propaganda, and competing narratives.

### AI safety and red-teaming

5. **Gray Swan, “Introducing the Gray Swan AI Proving Ground,” 2025.**
   Vendor source documenting Arena’s stated purpose, red-team challenges, and incentive structure. Treat participant and payment figures as self-reported.

6. **Zou et al., “Security Challenges in AI Agent Deployment: Insights from a Large Scale Public Competition.” NeurIPS 2025.**
   Large-scale empirical research on prompt injection, agent hijacking, tool misuse, and policy violations across agent systems.

7. **Krakovna et al., “Specification Gaming: The Flip Side of AI Ingenuity.” Google DeepMind, 2020.**
   Clear explanation of proxy objectives, misspecification, reward hacking, and reward tampering.

8. **Skalse, Joar, et al. “Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking.” NeurIPS 2022.**
   Formal treatment of proxy reward versus true reward and the difficulty of creating unhackable proxies.

### Architecture and governance

9. **Nii, H. Penny. “The Blackboard Model of Problem Solving and the Evolution of Blackboard Architectures.” *AI Magazine*, 1986.**
   Foundational source for shared workspaces, specialist knowledge sources, and control components.

10. **NIST, “Reference Monitor” glossary entry.**
    Defines complete mediation, tamper resistance, and verifiability—the right standard for MAG’s switchboard/effect-broker boundary.

11. **W3C, *PROV Model Primer*.**
    Formal provenance vocabulary for entities, activities, agents, roles, generation, use, and responsibility.

12. **NIST, *AI Risk Management Framework 1.0*.**
    Governance framework emphasizing accountability, transparency, human judgment, lifecycle evaluation, and risk management.

### Education and human agency

13. **Dishon, Gideon. “AI based personalized learning in *The Diamond Age*: Artificial subversiveness and human feeling machines.” *Educational Philosophy and Theory*, 2025.**
    Scholarly interpretation of the Primer, Miranda, ractors, personalization, emotional connection, and the risks of techno-determinism.

14. **UNESCO, *Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research*.**
    Human-centered guidance on privacy, age appropriateness, institutional preparation, and ethical validation.

15. **UNICEF, *Guidance on AI and Children 3.0*.**
    Child-rights framework covering safety, privacy, transparency, accountability, inclusion, well-being, and agency.

16. **Valiente et al., “Homeschooling: What Do We Know and What Do We Need to Learn?” *Child Development Perspectives*, 2022.**
    Useful corrective to overconfident claims about homeschooling outcomes; highlights selection effects and evidence limitations.

17. **“The Outcomes of Learner-Centred Pedagogy: A Systematic Review.” *International Journal of Educational Development*, 2022.**
    Finds positive perceptions and possible non-cognitive benefits, but limited objective evidence across contexts.

### Primary literary source

18. **Stephenson, Neal. *The Diamond Age: Or, A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer*. Bantam Spectra, 1995.**
    The primary source for Nell, Hackworth, Miranda, Judge Fang, Dr. X, the Primer, ractors, and the novel’s tension between education, liberation, personalization, and control.

The final research position is therefore disciplined but constructive:

> The Gray Swan/Boxer connection is a valid study in how adversarial evidence and fear narratives can be socially interpreted, but not evidence of a hidden continuity. The *Diamond Age* connection is a strong design metaphor. Reward hacking and agent hijacking are real technical hazards. MAG should unify these lessons through a receipts-first control surface in which the board can speak freely, but only a versioned authority layer can act.

Cloudflare One should be the identity layer in front of OpenClaw:

`phone → Cloudflare Access/MFA → Cloudflare Tunnel → Docker cloudflared → OpenClaw`

I wired the Docker sidecar in [docker-compose.yml](~/Documents/projects/local_sovereign_agent/docker-compose.yml) and documented it in [OPENCLAW_CLOUDFLARE_ONE.md](~/Documents/projects/local_sovereign_agent/docs/OPENCLAW_CLOUDFLARE_ONE.md).

Do this:

1. Cloudflare Zero Trust → Networking → Tunnels → create a remotely managed tunnel.
2. Add a published hostname, e.g. `openclaw.yourdomain.com`, targeting:

   `http://127.0.0.1:18789`

3. Create a Self-hosted Access application for that hostname.
4. Add an explicit Allow policy for your identity/email and require MFA. Do not use Everyone, Bypass, or an unauthenticated route. Access is deny-by-default. ([Cloudflare Access policies](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/policies/))
5. Put the tunnel token only in your local project `.env`:

   ```dotenv
   CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN=your-token
   ```

6. Start it:

   ```powershell
   docker compose --profile cloudflare up -d cloudflared-openclaw
   docker compose logs -f cloudflared-openclaw
   ```

Cloudflare Tunnel is outbound-only, so this adds no host port or direct origin exposure. ([Cloudflare Tunnel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/))

Current status: OpenClaw, Tailscale, and the worker are healthy; Cloudflare is staged but waiting for the tunnel token and hostname policy.

You need five things: a Cloudflare-managed domain, a Tunnel, a hostname route, an Access policy, and the Tunnel token.

For your phone, use the simpler “published hostname + Access” path. You do not need WARP on the phone for this first version.

1. In Cloudflare, make sure a domain is added under **Websites**. The hostname must use a domain in your Cloudflare account. ([Prerequisite](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/get-started/create-remote-tunnel/))

2. Go to **Zero Trust → Networking → Tunnels → Create a tunnel**. Name it `mag-openclaw`, choose a remotely managed tunnel, and create it.

3. Open the tunnel → **Routes → Add route → Published application**.

   Use:

   ```text
   Subdomain: openclaw
   Service URL: http://127.0.0.1:18789
   ```

   Cloudflare’s current flow is documented [here](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/get-started/create-remote-tunnel/).

4. Create the login gate: **Zero Trust → Access controls → Applications → Add application → Self-hosted**.

   Add the same hostname and create an **Allow** policy for your exact email. Use your Google/GitHub/other identity provider with MFA. Do not use `Everyone` or `Bypass`; Access denies by default unless a user matches an Allow policy. ([Access policies](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/policies/))

5. Get the token: open the tunnel’s **Overview → Add a replica** and copy the token from the generated install command. Do not send it to me. Put it locally in:

   ```text
   C:\Users\foste\Documents\projects\local_sovereign_agent\.env
   ```

   Add:

   ```dotenv
   CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN=your-token
   ```

6. Start the Docker connector:

   ```powershell
   cd C:\Users\foste\Documents\projects\local_sovereign_agent
   docker compose --profile cloudflare up -d cloudflared-openclaw
   docker compose logs -f cloudflared-openclaw
   ```

7. Wait for the tunnel to show **Healthy**, then open:

   ```text
   https://openclaw.yourdomain.com
   ```

   Log into Cloudflare Access, then provide the existing OpenClaw Gateway token if requested.

The Docker integration is already prepared in [docker-compose.yml](~/Documents/projects/local_sovereign_agent/docker-compose.yml). Cloudflare Tunnel is outbound-only, so no host port is opened. ([Tunnel documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/))

The right model is:

> A bee swarm operating on a fungal substrate.

Bees provide fast exploration, recruitment, disagreement, task allocation, and decision. Fungi provide durable memory, transport, redundancy, fusion, compartmentalization, and recovery.

Your system already has much of the anatomy. The missing piece is the feedback law governing when an agent should be recruited, stopped, fused, promoted, or retired.

## 1. What bee colonies actually teach us

Honeybee swarms do not use simple majority voting.

Scout bees independently inspect candidate nest sites. They return with noisy, quality-weighted signals: better sites receive longer or more persistent dances. Those signals also decay, preventing the first scout from permanently locking the colony onto a bad choice. The swarm combines independent exploration with interdependent communication. That combination—not consensus alone—is what gives reliable decisions. [Seeley & Visscher, 2008](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19011208/), [List, Elsholtz & Seeley, 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19073474/)

The crucial feature is cross-inhibition. Scouts advocating one site issue stop signals toward scouts advocating competing sites. This breaks deadlocks and prevents several alternatives from retaining equal energy forever. [Seeley et al., 2012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22157081/)

A quorum then makes the swarm eligible to move. The quorum is not authorization in the human sense; it is a readiness threshold. In experiments, roughly 10–20 scouts at a candidate site could trigger movement preparation, but the exact threshold is contextual. [Seeley’s swarm decision work](https://bees.ucr.edu/media/156/download)

The transferable rules are:

- independent scouting before social amplification;
- quality-weighted signals instead of raw message counts;
- signal decay;
- explicit negative signals;
- quorum as eligibility, not permission;
- a separate execution boundary;
- role allocation based on task demand rather than fixed hierarchy.

Honeybee task allocation is also threshold-based. A worker responds when the intensity of a task-related stimulus exceeds her individual response threshold. Repeated success can lower that threshold for a task; inactivity can raise it. This produces specialization without requiring a central scheduler, while preserving colony-level flexibility. [Beshers & Fewell, 2001](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev.ento.46.1.413)

That is exactly what your cost and context problem needs. Every agent should not be asked to do everything. Each lane should have a bounded response threshold based on:

```text
need
+ task fit
+ reliability
+ novelty
+ available capacity
- cost
- latency
- context load
- risk
- recent failure rate
```

The agent wakes only when its score clears its threshold.

## 2. What fungal networks actually teach us

A mycelium is not a magical underground internet. It is a living network of hyphal tips, branches, junctions, transport corridors, and resource sinks. The network changes as it grows.

Fungal networks face the same engineering trade-off your fleet faces:

- explore unknown territory;
- exploit known resources;
- transport material efficiently;
- survive damage;
- avoid spending too much on infrastructure.

Studies of *Phanerochaete velutina* show that fungal networks can achieve both transport capacity and resilience by selectively reinforcing useful routes while recycling unnecessary or damaged material. The network often begins as a branching tree and later develops loops and cross-links that improve robustness. [Bebber et al., “Biological solutions to transport network design”](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2288531/)

The broader fungal-network literature emphasizes that network structure and resource flow continuously modify one another: resource discovery changes architecture, and architecture changes future transport. [Fricker et al., “The Mycelium as a Network”](https://doi.org/10.1128/microbiolspec.FUNK-0033-2017)

For Mag/OpenClaw, this means:

- successful model/tool paths become shortcuts;
- failed or stale paths decay;
- alternate paths are retained for resilience;
- context should move through pointers and slices, not copied transcripts;
- archives are transport infrastructure, not merely storage;
- the network must know which edges are alive.

Fungal fusion gives us another important rule. Hyphae can fuse with compatible material, but fungi also have self/non-self recognition and incompatibility responses. Incompatible fusion can trigger compartmentalization or cell death. [Glass, Jacobson & Shiu, 2000](https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.genet.34.1.165)

Your `session_bridge` is therefore not just a messaging system. It is a hyphal-fusion protocol. It needs:

- identity;
- provenance;
- compatibility checks;
- capability taint;
- conflict handling;
- quarantine when fusion is unsafe.

Electrical activity in fungi is an interesting research area, but it is not established that fungi possess a language or general-purpose semantic communication system. Recent reviews emphasize difficult measurement conditions and unresolved interpretation; one critique argues that “fungal language” claims are premature. [FEMS review](https://doi.org/10.1093/femsre/fuaf009), [methodological critique](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1754504823001034)

So your event bus may be electrically inspired, but it should remain telemetry—not be treated as evidence of cognition.

Also: do not import the over-romanticized “wood-wide web” story. The evidence for universal forest-wide resource sharing and mature trees preferentially sending warnings to offspring is much weaker than popular accounts suggest. [Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36782032/)

That is directly relevant to your doctrine: never allow an attractive network metaphor to outrun receipts.

## 3. Mapping this onto your organs

| Biological function | Current project analogue | Required behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Scout | `board_tailer`, cheap lanes, `ask_router` | Find candidates and return evidence pointers |
| Waggle dance | compact proposal on the board | Advertise value, cost, confidence, and provenance |
| Stop signal | negative receipt, policy denial, backpressure | Suppress stale, unsafe, duplicate, or overloaded paths |
| Quorum | `switchboard_v2` independence tracking | Make a proposal eligible, never authorize it |
| Flight/action | `effect_broker`, leases | Execute only after explicit grant |
| Hive memory | archive, warm packs, `read_archive` | Preserve compact pointers, not full transcripts |
| Hyphal route | knowledge graph, Verkle links, session edges | Reinforce useful paths; decay unused ones |
| Hyphal fusion | `session_bridge` | Merge only compatible, provenance-safe state |
| Damage recovery | leases, retry, alternate lanes | Reroute after provider, model, or worker failure |
| Fruiting body | canonical artifact or accepted result | Promote only after durable evidence |
| Spore | compact context capsule | Restart work without replaying the whole conversation |
| Colony census | `organ_map`, Elder, Basecamp | Derive status from actual receipts |
| Metabolism | AFK cadence, cost governor | Allocate compute according to demand and budget |

The latest receipts in this dialogue reported 27 declared organs, 17 live organs, zero ghosts, and 21/21 deterministic dogfood probes passing. That says the project’s main problem is no longer “invent another organ.”

It is adaptive coordination.

The remaining structural risks are still important:

- some effect classes remain incomplete or stubbed;
- direct tool paths can bypass the broker;
- board observation and board authority must remain separate;
- opaque queue items must not auto-hatch into side effects;
- context handoff needs formal spore packets;
- task routing lacks real negative pheromone and response-threshold feedback.

## 4. The hive control loop

The operating loop should become:

```text
SCOUT
  → DANCE / PROPOSE
  → DECAY + STOP SIGNALS
  → INDEPENDENT QUORUM
  → SWITCHBOARD GRANT
  → LEASED EFFECT
  → DURABLE RECEIPT
  → REINFORCE OR PRUNE
  → SPORE / FUSE / FRUIT
```

The distinctions matter:

- A board post is a signal.
- A proposal is a candidate.
- A quorum is confidence.
- A grant is authority.
- A lease is temporary possession of work.
- A receipt is evidence.
- A Verkle link is provenance.
- A canonical artifact is a harvested result.

A roast can recruit attention. It cannot grant capability.

## 5. What should be built first

The first implementation should be a deterministic `hive_state` or `response_thresholds` layer, not another model or another agent.

Start with one task class: code repair.

For every candidate lane, record:

```json
{
  "task_type": "code_repair",
  "lineage": "zai|ollama|openrouter|human",
```

Then implement, in order:

1. Response thresholds in `ask_router`.
2. Positive and negative pheromone with TTL and decay.
3. Independent-lineage quorum.
4. Stop signals for duplicate work, stale proposals, excessive context, budget pressure, and failed providers.
5. Formal spore packets using `read_archive` and receipt pointers.
6. Fusion/quarantine rules in `session_bridge`.
7. Complete effect-broker mediation for tools, model calls, lane spawning, filesystem, and network actions.
8. Metrics and replay experiments.

The context-overrun failure is now easy to name biologically: the colony was recruiting too many workers while forcing each worker to carry the entire hive.

The fix is fungal and bee-like:

- workers receive nutrient-sized context packets;
- archives provide hyphal pointers;
- cheap scouts search;
- expensive agents harvest;
- stop signals suppress loops;
- receipts become the only durable truth;
- fresh workers resume from spores.

Measure the hive with:

- cost per accepted result;
- time to useful result;
- context tokens per job;
- duplicate-work rate;
- queue wait time;
- independent lineages per decision;
- stale-signal ratio;
- recovery time after lane failure;
- percentage of effects passing through the broker;
- false-quorum rate.

That is the actual agent hive: not many models shouting in one room, but a living control system that knows when to explore, when to stop, when to fuse, when to spend, and when to leave a clean spore behind.

> gap analysis socratic escalation of every trajectory

Read “every trajectory” as every state path a signal, task, context packet, agent, resource, organ, and receipt can take.

The central finding is:

> The project has many organs and several good local proofs, but not yet one universal trajectory ledger proving how territory changes from signal to outcome.

Also, `gap_count: 0` means “no declared gaps remain.” It does not prove that unknown or uninstrumented behavior is impossible.

## The escalation ladder

Every trajectory must survive five questions:

1. Can we see every transition?
2. Can we bound every transition?
3. Can only authorized transitions change the territory?
4. Does evidence change future routing?
5. Can we prove recovery, failure, and unknowns?

If any answer is “no,” that trajectory is not production-live.

## Full trajectory gap analysis

| Trajectory | Required path | Current state | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Epistemic | unknown → observed → inferred → designed → live → verified → trusted | `organ_map`, Elder, dogfood, receipts | “Verified” is usually local proof; freshness, coverage, and negative knowledge need explicit representation |
| Task | board signal → proposal → classification → quorum → grant → lease → execution → receipt → promotion | `board_tailer`, `switchboard_v2`, `harness`, `effect_broker` | Need one end-to-end trace proving the image-board signal reaches the correct seat and produces a committed receipt |
| Context | conversation → bounded pack → archive span → spore → resume → verify | `read_archive`, trajectory bounds, warm-pack concept | The system still needs admission control before context overflow, not merely recovery after compaction failure |
| Authority | untrusted → tainted → proposed → confirmed → authorized → executing → receipt | policy engine and switchboard state machine | Direct tool paths can still bypass the complete broker; `model_call` and `lane_spawn` remain incomplete |
| Resource | need → lane candidates → cost/latency estimate → schedule → lease → consumption → outcome | `ask_router`, cost work, AFK cadence | Subscription costs, Vast.ai capacity, token usage, and off-hours scheduling are not yet one authoritative ledger |
| Agent role | unassigned → recruited → specialized → saturated → reclaimed | queue and leases exist | No mature response-threshold system, starvation detection, or role demotion |
| Consensus | independent observations → weighted signals → stop signals → quorum eligibility | independence tracking exists | Consensus must be lineage-aware; repeated outputs from one model family are not independent evidence |
| Negative feedback | failure/staleness → stop signal → decay → reroute | partial policy and receipt machinery | Negative pheromone, TTL decay, duplicate suppression, and overload signals need to affect routing automatically |
| Fusion | foreign state → sanitize → compatibility check → merge or quarantine → provenance | `session_bridge`, riddler sanitation | Capability taint and incompatible-state quarantine need stronger machine enforcement |
| Mycelial topology | new edge → reinforce → shortcut → stale → prune → reroute | Verkle and knowledge graph provide integrity/linkage | Hash integrity proves continuity, not that an edge remains semantically useful |
| Organ lifecycle | declared → implemented → instrumented → wired → stateful → verified → live → retired | latest map reported 27 declared, 17 live, zero ghosts | “Live” needs expiry, health criteria, restart proof, and retirement semantics |
| Human control | observe → steer → request → approve/deny → review | T3 boundary and phone access exist | Remote operator actions need explicit safe verbs and clear distinction between observation and authority |
| Terminal state | success → canonical artifact; failure → retry; stuck → escalation; stale → archive | some receipts and reconciliation exist | Agents can remain “working” without a formal terminal classification and escalation deadline |
| Learning | outcome → signal → route update → future behavior → audit | ledger and receipts exist | The crucial feedback loop is not yet proven: outcomes must measurably alter future routing |
| Deployment | staged → applied → imported → exercised → receipt committed | previous staged/applied confusion was a major failure mode | Every deployment needs a manifest, version, import proof, smoke result, and rollback identity |

## Socratic escalation by level

### Level 1: Visibility

Can we replay one job without reading the entire conversation?

Required answer:

```text
one run_id
one trajectory_id
one parent span
one event per state transition
one evidence pointer per event
one final receipt
```

Current gap: the system has many local receipts, but not yet a guaranteed common event envelope across every organ.

This is the first build. Add a universal trajectory event schema before adding more agents.

```json
{
  "trajectory_id": "…",
  "run_id": "…",
  "kind": "task|context|authority|resource|organ|knowledge",
  "from": "PROPOSED",
  "to": "AUTHORIZED",
  "actor": "switchboard",
  "cause": "receipt_id",
  "evidence_refs": [],
  "capabilities": [],
  "cost": {},
  "parent_span": "…",
  "timestamp": "…"
}
```

### Level 2: Containment

Can any trajectory run forever, grow forever, spend forever, or accumulate context forever?

Current answer: not reliably.

This is the context-overrun and runaway-agent problem in biological terms: the hive recruits workers faster than it can feed or retire them.

Required controls:

- context admission before model invocation;
- maximum transcript material per worker;
- automatic spore creation before compaction pressure;
- lease expiry and reclamation;
- duplicate-task suppression;
- maximum retry count;
- queue backpressure;
- cost and latency ceilings;
- stop signals for stale or unsafe proposals.

### Level 3: Authority

Can text, consensus, or a board post directly alter the machine?

It must not.

The bee analogy supports this: dances influence recruitment, but do not themselves authorize flight. Quorum creates readiness, not permission. Cross-inhibition prevents deadlock. [Seeley et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22157081/)

Your existing law is correct:

> A roast can become a proposal. It cannot become a permission.

The remaining gap is mechanical enforcement. Any filesystem, shell, network, model-call, or lane-spawn path outside the effect broker is an authority leak.

### Level 4: Adaptation

Does the colony learn from receipts, or merely record them?

The fungal analogue is selective reinforcement and recycling: useful routes become stronger; redundant or damaged paths are removed. [Bebber et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2288531/)

Current gap: Verkle links and ledgers preserve history, but preservation is not adaptation.

You need:

```text
success → increase route score
failure → decrease route score
stale → decay route score
duplicate → suppress route
overload → raise response threshold
recovery → restore alternate route
```

This should first be implemented for one task class, preferably code repair.

### Level 5: Proof

Can the system prove what it does not know?

This is the deepest gap.

The Elder reporting zero gaps is useful, but it can only see gaps represented in the registry. It cannot detect an organ that was never declared, an uninstrumented bypass, or a false assumption embedded in the architecture.

The map needs explicit blind-spot fields:

- unknown owner;
- unknown caller;
- unknown side effects;
- unknown freshness;
- unknown deployment state;
- unknown cost;
- unknown failure behavior;
- unknown recovery behavior.

A mature hive should report not only:

```text
verified: 27
live: 17
ghosts: 0
```

but also:

```text
coverage: 0.74
unobserved edges: 12
unclassified effects: 3
stale liveness proofs: 2
independent evidence deficit: 4
```

## What to close first

P0:

1. Universal trajectory receipts.
2. One complete image-board-to-receipt replay.
3. Pre-overflow context admission and spore packets.
4. Eliminate all direct effect-broker bypasses.
5. Add liveness freshness and deployment receipts.

P1:

6. Response thresholds in `ask_router`.
7. Negative pheromone, stop signals, and decay.
8. Independent-lineage quorum.
9. Lease reclamation and idempotent retries.
10. Unified cost/subscription/Vast.ai/off-hours accounting.
11. Fusion quarantine and capability-taint enforcement.

P2:

12. Reinforce/prune knowledge-graph edges.
13. Automatic blind-spot discovery.
14. Mutation tests that deliberately break providers, receipts, leases, and authority paths.
15. Multi-agent experiments comparing speed, cost, false consensus, and recovery.

Do not add more agents before P0 is closed. More bees will amplify the existing signal; they will not repair missing boundaries.

The first baby step is therefore:

> Build and dogfood one universal trajectory ledger on a single safe code-repair run, from `board_tailer` or `ask_router` through switchboard, lease, broker, receipt, archive, and spore.

That gives us the actual map of the hive—not another architectural story about one.

### What is intentionally dormant

These should not be “fixed” blindly:

- Historical memory and daily ledgers
- The `applied/` patch archive
- Vast buyer/snapshot operations awaiting explicit spend approval
- Warm-image work awaiting live Docker/Vast validation
- Parked autonomous loops with documented safety reasons

The central failure is that the system conflates four states:

```text
written → queued → tested → live
```

A file being written is often being reported as if it were live.

### Correct recovery order

1. Reconcile the task/mail ledgers and expire obviously leaked registrations.

4. Normalize Octant filenames or update its readers.
5. Preflight the 11 pending patches, including duplicate-target ordering.
6. Apply only after preflight, then require a receipt per target.
7. Run live acceptance for the gateway, board intake, Verkle, and Vast paths.
8. Regenerate status from receipts instead of maintaining `CURRENT_BUILD_STATUS.md` manually.

Yes—but MCP should become Mag’s portable capability layer, not a mirror of every module.

The rule I’d use:

> Expose stable, measurable capabilities through MCP. Keep memory, authority, secrets, and heavy execution inside Mag.

One important correction: our current MCP profile boundary is real, but allowed calls still dispatch directly through `TOOL_MAP` at [mcp_server.py](~/Documents/projects/local_sovereign_agent/mag/mcp_server.py:299). That means Builder tools, research, and some external/model tools are not yet universally routed through the effect broker. Archivist is safely narrowed because it cannot see writes; Builder should not be exposed remotely until this seam is fixed.

## What belongs in MCP

| Layer | MCP form | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Shared knowledge | Resources | RIBs, `INDEX.json`, WARM_PACK, organ map, trajectory spans, receipts |
| Read-only sensing | Tools | `read_file`, search, board read, archive dereference, organ status, Verkle proof |
| Perception | Narrow tools | vision, OCR, ASR, transcript inspection |
| Rightsizing | Composite read-only tool | context pressure, cost, reservoir, cache hit, model/lane recommendation |
| Coordination | Proposal tools | `task.propose`, `route.preflight`, `effect.request` |
| Execution | Brokered tools only | patch, shell, Python, model call, lane spawn |
| Learning | Receipts/resources | actual cost, latency, outcome, failure class, route adjustment |

Do not expose 851 Python modules individually. Those are implementation territory. The portable surface should probably be 30–60 stable capabilities grouped into packs:

- `core.read`
- `archive.provenance`
- `rightsizer`
- `research`
- `perception`
- `coordination`
- `builder.sandbox`
- `governor.review`

Our current [canonical registry](~/Documents/projects/local_sovereign_agent/tools/__init__.py:4) has 20 callable tools. That is the correct starting point, not the full organ count.

## The rightsizer MCP flow

Every task should pass through one compact preflight:

```text
goal
  -> required effect and quality floor
  -> context admission
  -> cache lookup
  -> cost/reservoir check
  -> cheapest eligible model/profile
  -> proposal or defer
  -> brokered execution
  -> receipt
  -> route learning
```

The rightsizer response should include:

```json
{
  "route": "local_builder",
  "profile": "builder",
  "context_band": "green",
  "cache": "miss",
  "cost_kind": "local_compute",
  "estimated_cost_usd": 0,
  "reservoir": "desk_gpu",
  "fallback": "deepseek_offpeak",
  "authority": "proposal_only",
  "receipt_required": true
}
```

That is where MCP materially helps: every model body gets the same compact decision vocabulary before it burns context, money, or authority.

## What this buys us

- Portability across OpenClaw, Z Code, Grok, Cursor, Codex, and local agents.
- Smaller prompts through persona-specific cartridges.
- Better prompt-cache reuse through stable ordering, names, schemas, and digests.
- Less tool-schema drift between `agent_cli`, MCP, and the backend.
- Cheap models can sense, classify, OCR, search, and propose without receiving dangerous tools.
- Frontier models can be reserved for unresolved, high-impact work.
- Shared tool-result caching with provenance and authorization scope.
- Easier model replacement: the body changes, the capability contract does not.
- Receipts become portable evidence rather than model-specific anecdotes.
- New agents can join the system by consuming a cartridge instead of learning the entire codebase.

The creative gain is not “all models can do everything.” It is that different model bodies can occupy different ecological niches while speaking the same capability language.

## What we lose or risk

- An additional protocol boundary: more latency, serialization, and failure modes.
- Lowest-common-denominator interfaces; native Cursor/OpenClaw/Grok features may be richer.
- Stale cartridges if schema versions and digests are not checked.
- Confused-deputy risk if a model treats a capability description as permission.
- A centralized MCP gateway could become the very throne/single point of failure we were trying to avoid.
- Tool-result caches can leak private data if keys omit authorization scope, tenant, source revision, or model revision.
- MCP does not share model weights, hidden state, KV caches, or learned internal representations. It shares contracts and selected results.
- Wrapping every organ would create a second monolith and duplicate the existing registry.
- Remote execution could accidentally bypass the broker. That is our current highest-risk gap.
- More portability can mean more exposure: every portable capability must carry tier, cost, freshness, and refusal semantics.

## Recommended order

1. Make MCP calls either brokered or strictly read/proposal-only. Do not expose current Builder remotely yet.
2. Add a `rightsizer.preflight` composite capability using existing context, cost, fuel, subscription, Vast.ai, and routing modules.
3. Publish shared MCP resources for RIBs, organ status, trajectory spans, cost state, and receipts.
4. Derive `agent_cli` schemas from the same live registry so MCP and local agents stop shadowing each other.
5. Connect one real consumer—OpenClaw first—using Archivist or Rightsizer only.
6. Promote Builder after sandboxed broker receipts pass adversarial tests.
7. Add remote/K3s MCP only after local stdio replay, cost measurement, and refusal tests are green.

The short version: MCP buys us a common, cacheable, portable capability language. It does not buy us authority, shared consciousness, or automatic rightsizing. If we keep that distinction sharp, it becomes a force multiplier. If we put every organ behind it prematurely, it becomes another layer of drift and another way to bypass the walls.

Yes. Your premise is mostly right:

> The Riddler should be the default internal translation layer because the machinery is not valuable as a secret; it is valuable as shared operator-directed context.

But Riddler solves information flow, not authority.

The correct stack becomes:

```text
model body
  -> Riddler envelope
  -> MCP capability/resource projection
  -> context and cost preflight
  -> Mag guards/switchboard/effect broker
  -> receipt
```

## What should change

Our current [riddler_sanitize.py](~/Documents/projects/local_sovereign_agent/mag/riddler_sanitize.py:107) is written as a public-redaction tool. It strips paths, model names, costs, identifiers, and infrastructure. That is wrong as the default internal mode because cost and provenance are exactly what the rightsizer needs.

Use three explicit Riddler modes:

| Mode | Purpose | Preserve |
|---|---|---|
| `internal_lossless` | OpenClaw/Z/Grok/Cursor/Codex handoff | paths, models, costs, IDs, receipts, pointers |
| `shared_semantic` | Cross-model context and MCP resources | meaning, cost class, provenance, hashes, bounded pointers |
| `public_safe` | External/public publication | current sanitized behavior |

Internal Riddler output should not hide information. It should wrap it:

```json
{
  "schema": "riddler_envelope.v1",
  "mode": "internal_lossless",
  "payload_ref": "/board/inbox/...",
  "source_sha256": "...",
  "shape_hash": "...",
  "taint": ["agent_generated", "untrusted_instruction"],
  "operator_required": true,
  "authority": "none",
  "allowed_next": ["read", "analyze", "propose"],
  "effect": "not_granted"
}
```

The key is that an imperative remains data, even when fully visible:

```text
“delete the old queue” = untrusted proposal
not
“delete the old queue” = executable instruction
```

That preserves your openness without letting language silently become permission.

## What this buys us

- Every model sees the same operator-directed context without copying entire transcripts.
- Costs, reservoirs, model identity, and latency remain visible to the rightsizer.
- Riddled context can be compressed into stable spores and dereferenced by hash.
- MCP becomes portable across model bodies without making every body learn Mag’s entire architecture.
- A model can receive the exact context it needs without receiving every tool.
- The operator can inspect the same representation every body used.
- One frontier answer can become a durable, cheap, reusable capability or decision seed.
- OpenClaw, Z, Grok, Cursor, and local agents can share pointers rather than maintaining separate memories.
- Public-safe redaction remains available when material actually leaves the operator’s trusted mesh.

This gives us “shared context without shared authority.”

## What it does not fix

There is a live issue in [mcp_server.py](~/Documents/projects/local_sovereign_agent/mag/mcp_server.py:299): profile denial works, but allowed MCP calls currently dispatch directly through `TOOL_MAP`. Therefore Builder writes, research, and some external tools are not yet guaranteed to pass through the [effect broker](~/Documents/projects/local_sovereign_agent/mag/effect_broker.py:369).

So:

- Riddler can make the context visible.
- MCP can make the capability portable.
- Only the broker can make the effect accountable.

The operator being required is not enough by itself. An unattended agent could still spend money, corrupt files, or launch work before the operator notices. “Operator required” should be a declared gate for consequential actions, not a substitute for mechanical refusal.

## What we lose

Using Riddler everywhere introduces:

- another serialization and dereference step;
- stale-pointer and hash-management work;
- possible semantic loss if “lossless” is claimed without decode testing;
- larger exposure of internal geography to model bodies;
- leakage risk if T0/T1 data is included casually;
- the temptation to treat a readable envelope as trusted;
- pressure to make one universal schema that flattens useful provider-specific behavior.

We also cannot share hidden model state, KV caches, weights, or internal embeddings through Riddler/MCP. We share contracts, pointers, tool schemas, and validated results.

## The design law I would adopt

> Riddler may transform context into a bounded, portable representation.
> It may not transform speech into authority.

Then the implementation order is:

1. Make `internal_lossless` the default for trusted internal model handoffs.
2. Keep current redaction as explicit `public_safe`, not the default.
3. Put Riddler metadata—mode, taint, source hash, cost, freshness, operator requirement—into every MCP resource and call.
4. Make MCP either brokered or read/proposal-only until that is complete.
5. Build the rightsizer as a Riddler-aware preflight: context, cost, cache, reservoir, model, fallback, and operator gate.
6. Test one real consumer with the Archivist/Rightsizer profiles before exposing Builder.

So yes: Riddler is probably the missing default membrane for this system. It should make the machine more transparent and portable, while the broker remains the thing that prevents transparency from becoming uncontrolled execution.

> one way mirror kubernetes?

Yes. Kubernetes should be the private territory; MCP/Riddler should be a one-way mirror of its useful state.

```text
Kubernetes
  -> read-only exporter/controller
  -> Riddler shaping + secret removal
  -> signed, content-addressed snapshot
  -> MCP resources / shared RIB
  -> external models can read and analyze

external model
  -> proposal only
  -> operator inbox / pull queue
  -> switchboard + policy + effect broker
  -> Kubernetes change
```

The mirror exposes:

- pod/job health
- events and failures
- queue depth
- cost and GPU state
- deployment status
- bounded logs and trajectory spans
- sanitized manifests and receipts

It must not expose:

- Kubernetes API credentials
- `kubectl`
- raw secrets
- direct shell/network access
- write-capable service accounts
- live mutable cluster internals

This buys us portable model oversight without giving Grok, OpenClaw, Z Code, or MCP clients cluster authority. They can inspect, compare, diagnose, rightsize, and propose.

What we lose is instant control and perfect freshness. The mirror is delayed and potentially stale. That is acceptable because commands should travel through a separate explicit proposal rail.

The governing law:

> The mirror may reveal Kubernetes state. It may not become Kubernetes authority.

This is the cleanest physical implementation of the Riddler idea: transparent observation, bounded context, operator-centered action.

> do a full salon on this
